name: TCS
summary: TCS hires most freshers in India through the TCS National Qualifier Test (NQT), a computer-based test run through TCS iON, followed by interviews that candidates commonly describe as technical, managerial and HR rounds, often on the same day. The interviews usually stay close to fundamentals (OOP, DBMS, SQL, one programming language), your resume and your final-year project, with HR questions on relocation and shifts.
rounds: TCS NQT (aptitude, reasoning, verbal and coding)
looks_for: Fundamentals: OOP, DBMS, a programming language, your final-year project
Willingness to relocate and work in shifts

questions.text: Tell me about yourself.
covers: Your degree, college and the one or two skills you're strongest in
Your best project or internship in two sentences, with your own part in it
Why you're applying for this role, all in under two minutes

questions.text: Explain your final-year project and your part in it.
covers: The problem it solved and who would use it
How it works in plain words: front end, back end, database, any outside services
What you built yourself, one difficulty you hit and how you solved it

questions.text: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
covers: An abstract class can hold state and some implemented methods; an interface mainly defines a contract
A class extends one class but can implement many interfaces (in Java or C#), and how default methods blur the line
When you'd choose each, with a small example such as shapes or payment methods

questions.text: Are you willing to relocate and work in any shift?
covers: A clear, honest answer: yes, or yes with a real constraint stated politely
That you understand client work can follow other time zones
Something that shows you adapt well, such as studying or working away from home

questions.text: Why do you want to join TCS?
covers: One or two specific reasons: training for new joiners, the range of industries it serves, moving across technologies
How that fits what you want to learn in your first few years
Something you've read about its work, not general praise for its size

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new tool or language quickly.
covers: Why you needed it and how little time you had
How you learned it: documentation, small experiments, asking someone
What you delivered with it and what you'd do faster next time

questions.text: Tell me about a disagreement in a team project and how it was resolved.
covers: What the disagreement was about, described fairly from both sides
What you said or did to move it forward, such as testing both ideas
How it ended and how the team worked together afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you balanced your studies with another big responsibility.
covers: The two commitments, such as a club, sport, part-time work or family duty
How you planned your time and what you gave up
The result for both, and what it taught you about deadlines

questions.text: What is one weakness you're working on, and what are you doing about it?
covers: A real weakness that matters at work, not a disguised strength
A specific example of when it caused a problem
The steps you're taking and the progress you can show

questions.text: What is the difference between a primary key, a unique key and a foreign key?
covers: Primary key: identifies each row, no nulls, one per table
Unique key: no duplicates but can usually allow a null; a table can have several
Foreign key: links to another table's key, with an example such as orders and customers

questions.text: What happens, step by step, when you type a website address into a browser and press Enter?
covers: DNS lookup to find the server's IP address
Opening a connection (TCP, and TLS for HTTPS), then the HTTP request and response
The browser rendering HTML, CSS and JavaScript and fetching other files

questions.text: A client's banking application becomes slow every month-end. How would you start finding the cause?
covers: Asking what 'slow' means: which screens, which users, since when
Checking what is different at month-end: batch jobs, report queries, traffic
Looking at logs and database query times before guessing, then a fix and a check

questions.text: For experienced candidates: tell me about a production issue on your project and how your team handled it.
covers: What broke, who was affected and how it was noticed
Your part in finding the cause and fixing it
What changed afterwards to stop it recurring, such as a test, alert or process

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?
covers: One or two thoughtful questions about the training, the first project or the team
Nothing you could easily find on the careers site
A short thank-you and a line on why you're still keen

tips: Know your project inside out: they'll ask what you built yourself.
Revise OOP, DBMS and SQL basics; expect one or two simple coding questions.
Answer HR questions honestly and briefly; relocation and bond questions are common.
Read the current NQT pattern on the official registration page before you prepare; sections and timings can change between cycles.
Draw your project's flow on paper beforehand: modules, database tables, and who did what.
In the managerial round, expect a 'what would you do' scenario; reason aloud and say how you'd keep the client informed.
If you don't know an answer, say so and explain how you'd find out; guessing on a basic concept costs more.

rounds: Online application, with an online test for some graduate roles
Technical interview on your skills and past projects
Managerial interview (for some roles, a client interview as well)
